Psychometrics and assessment

How psychology measures: reliability, validity, norms, interviews and responsible interpretation of results.

Level 1 · Short introduction

Psychometrics is the discipline that designs and checks psychological measurement instruments: tests, questionnaires and scales. Psychological assessment combines them with interviews and observation to understand a person and make decisions. A good test must measure consistently (reliability) and measure what it claims to measure (validity).

Level 2 · Fuller explanation

Reliability

A test is reliable if it gives similar results when repeated under similar conditions, if its items are consistent with one another and if different assessors reach similar conclusions. Every measurement has a margin of error, and it is worth knowing.

Validity

This is the most important question: do the scores mean what we think they mean? It is checked by seeing whether the content is appropriate, whether scores relate to what they should (for example, a depression test to clinical diagnosis) and whether they do not relate to what they should not.

Norms

A score on its own says little. To interpret it, it is compared with that of a reference group of the same age, sex or education. That is why a well-built test states which population it was normed on and when.

More than tests

The interview is the most widely used tool. Structured interviews, with fixed questions, are more reliable than unstructured ones. Observation and self-monitoring records complete the picture. No score replaces professional judgement or the person's history.

Responsible interpretation

Results must be explained to the person assessed, protected as confidential data and not used for purposes other than those for which they were collected.

Screening and diagnosis

A screening questionnaire, such as the PHQ-9 for depression, is used to identify who should be assessed more thoroughly, not to diagnose. Two key concepts: sensitivity (how many real cases it detects) and specificity (how many people without the problem it correctly rules out). No test is perfect on both, and the cut-off is chosen according to which error matters more.

Adapting a test to another language

Translating a questionnaire is not enough. It must be checked that the questions mean the same in another culture, that the structure holds and that local norms exist. That is why the International Test Commission guidelines call for translation and back-translation, pilot studies and equivalence analyses.

Tests on the internet

Many tests circulating online have no reliability or validity studies. A good clue is to check whether the test has an identifiable author, scientific publications supporting it and a clear explanation of what it measures and what it does not.

Response scales

Many questionnaires ask people to rate agreement with a statement on a five- or seven-point scale, from "strongly disagree" to "strongly agree". This is the Likert scale, proposed by Rensis Likert in 1932. It looks simple, but its design matters: the number of options, whether there is a midpoint, how the ends are labelled and whether some items are reverse-worded to detect people who always answer the same way.

Answering to look good

When we answer a questionnaire we do not just inform: we also present ourselves. Social desirability leads people to exaggerate the positive and keep quiet about what is frowned upon, such as alcohol use. Others tend to agree with almost everything (acquiescence) or always use the extremes. Good tests include ways of detecting these response styles, and guaranteeing anonymity reduces the problem.

When a change matters

If someone drops three points on a depression questionnaire, have they really improved? It may be a change within measurement error. That is why the reliable change is calculated, taking the test's reliability into account, together with the minimal clinically important difference, the smallest change patients perceive as meaningful. Both concepts help interpret scores in the clinic and in trials.

Level 3 · Going further, with references

Classical test theory, formulated in the early twentieth century from Charles Spearman's work, assumes that every observed score is the sum of a true score and an error. In 1951 Lee Cronbach proposed the alpha coefficient to estimate internal consistency, and in 1955, with Paul Meehl, the concept of construct validity. Samuel Messick later argued that validity concerns the use and interpretation of scores, including their consequences.

Item response theory models the probability of answering each item correctly according to the person's level and the item's characteristics. It makes it possible to build computer adaptive tests, which choose the next question according to previous answers and achieve precise measurement with fewer items.

Not all famous tests are well supported. The Rorschach inkblot test (1921), for example, has limited validity for many of the uses it was put to, though some recent scoring systems have improved its reliability. In Spain, the General Council of Psychology regularly reviews the quality of tests published in the country following the European EFPA model.

Open debates: test fairness across cultural and linguistic groups; the use of artificial intelligence and digital data to assess people; and how to prevent misuse of tests in recruitment or the courts.

Item response theory

Classical psychometrics focuses on the total score. Item response theory analyses each question: its difficulty and how well it distinguishes between people at different levels. It makes it possible to create computerised adaptive tests, which choose the next question based on previous answers and achieve the same precision with fewer questions. Many international exams and modern clinical scales, such as those of the PROMIS project, use it.

Assessment and fairness

Tests can be unfair if they favour one group for reasons unrelated to what they measure, for example vocabulary or cultural familiarity. Differential item functioning analyses detect questions that behave differently in groups with the same true level. The Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing (2014) set out these requirements.

Measuring in real life

Asking "how have you felt this month?" depends on memory, which is swayed by recent days and the most intense moments. Ecological momentary assessment asks people to respond several times a day, usually on their phone, to brief questions about what they feel and do at that moment. It shows how mood, pain or the urge to smoke change across the day and in different contexts.

Tests that adapt

Thanks to item response theory, a computer can choose each question based on previous answers, as a good oral examiner does. These computerised adaptive tests achieve the same precision with far fewer questions. The PROMIS system, funded by the US National Institutes of Health, uses them to measure symptoms such as pain, fatigue or anxiety with four to twelve questions.
